findings.title: Backup-code login can bypass password check with dummy totpCode
findings.body: authorize() only verifies the password when `!credentials.totpCode` (line 121), but the backup-code branch is taken whenever `credentials.backupCode` is truthy without requiring totpCode to be empty. An attacker who knows a valid backup code can send email + valid backupCode + any dummy totpCode, which skips password verification and then succeeds on backup-code check alone without ever verifying password or TOTP. Consequence is second-factor-only login: password is not required, so a leaked or guessed 10-char backup code alone yields account takeover.

findings.title: Backup codes stored with reversible encryption instead of hash
findings.body: Backup codes are persisted with symmetricEncrypt, which is reversible with CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY, and later decrypted for comparison. Unlike the TOTP secret which must be reversible, backup codes only need comparison and should be one-way hashed like passwords. Consequence is that any database plus encryption-key compromise exposes all long-lived backup codes in plaintext, allowing persistent bypass of the authenticator.

findings.title: Backup-code check-then-update race allows reuse
findings.body: Login reads the decrypted backupCodes array, finds the matching index, then in a separate prisma.user.update writes the array back with that entry nulled. Two concurrent authorize() calls with the same code can both pass the indexOf check before either write completes, so both succeed. Consequence is the exactly-once guarantee for backup codes is broken under concurrency.

findings.title: Lost-access toggle button unintentionally submits disable form
findings.body: The Lost access / Go back button is rendered inside the Form that handles disable but has no type="button" and no preventDefault, so browsers treat it as type submit. Clicking it to switch between TOTP and backup-code inputs also triggers handleDisable with empty codes. Consequence is spurious disable requests and confusing incorrect-code errors when the user only intended to switch modes.

findings.title: Download backup-codes button also submits enable form
findings.body: The download link and Button are inside the Form whose submit handler verifies the TOTP code, but unlike the Copy and Close buttons which call preventDefault, the Download button has no type button handling or preventDefault. Clicking Download therefore also submits the enable form with the stale totpCode. Consequence is duplicate enable API calls on every download, possible error states on the backup-codes screen where no error is displayed.

findings.title: Throwing Error instead of JSON response breaks client handling
findings.body: When the encryption key is missing or the 2FA secret is missing the handler does throw new Error(ErrorCode.InternalServerError) instead of returning res.status(500).json({error}). An uncaught throw in a Next.js API route produces a non-JSON 500 page, while the modal client always does await response.json() and expects {error}. Consequence is unhandled exceptions, failed JSON parsing, and generic UI failure instead of a structured error.

findings.title: Backup-code verification is case and whitespace sensitive
findings.body: Generated codes are lowercase hex displayed as XXXXX-XXXXX, but verification only does replaceAll("-","") with no trim or toLowerCase, same pattern in the disable endpoint. A user typing uppercase, pasting with spaces, newlines, or surrounding whitespace gets IncorrectBackupCode even with a correct code. Consequence is legitimate backup codes are rejected and users can be locked out when they most need recovery.

findings.title: Used codes nulled not removed so exhaustion never detected
findings.body: After a successful backup-code login the code sets backupCodes[index] = null and re-encrypts the same-length array. After all 10 codes are used the column is still a non-null JSON array of nulls, so the MissingBackupCodes check for !user.backupCodes never fires and later attempts always return IncorrectBackupCode. Consequence is stale data accumulates and users get a misleading error with no signal that they are out of codes and must re-generate via disable/enable.

findings.title: No coverage for login or disable with backup code
findings.body: This PR adds backup-code authentication in next-auth, the login page Lost access flow, and the disable-with-backup-code endpoint, but the e2e only exercises download, copy, and close of the backup-codes dialog and explicitly leaves a TODO for login plus disabling with backup. Consequence is single-use invalidation, password interaction, and IncorrectBackupCode/MissingBackupCodes paths ship untested.
